analysis.one_liner: Stops companies from using bankruptcy to shield parent firms from injury lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 20, 2026, with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Some large companies facing mass injury lawsuits, such as talc or asbestos claims, restructure into new corporate forms and file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy so the bankruptcy court's automatic freeze on lawsuits (the "stay") blocks claims against their parent companies too. This bill would let courts throw out bankruptcy filings made in bad faith or that have no real chance of reorganizing the company, and would stop the bankruptcy stay from freezing lawsuits against a debtor's parent companies, insurers, and other non-debtor entities in cases involving injury claims affecting 100 or more people. It would also treat a debtor as acting in bad faith if it deliberately manufactured the bankruptcy's location through a corporate split.
analysis.who_benefits: People with injury or toxic-exposure claims against large companies, including mass-tort claimants who currently see their lawsuits frozen for years behind a bankruptcy stay. It also helps the creditors' committees and individual creditors whose cases are prolonged by filings courts judge futile.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes a Chapter 11 filing that is objectively futile or in subjective bad faith a ground for the court to dismiss the case, so companies cannot file simply to run out the clock on creditors and claimants [S2].

It stops the bankruptcy automatic stay from freezing lawsuits against non-debtor entities — parent companies, officers, insurers, and lenders tied to the debtor — when those suits involve injury, contamination, or exposure claims affecting at least 100 people [S2].

It creates a presumption that a filing is in bad faith if the court finds the debtor manufactured the bankruptcy's venue, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence, and an automatic bad-faith presumption when the debtor was formed or restructured through a divisional merger within four years before filing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large companies facing mass-tort liability, their parent companies and affiliates, their insurers, and the lenders and advisors who finance liability-capping restructurings. Some of those costs could ultimately be passed to consumers and employees if companies face higher legal exposure.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies a conclusive presumption of bad faith to any debtor that underwent a divisional merger or major restructuring within four years of filing, which could sweep up legitimate reorganizations and make Chapter 11 riskier for companies in genuine distress [S2].

Companies facing hopeless mass-tort liability might respond by liquidating instead of reorganizing, which can leave employees without jobs and, in some cases, leave all creditors — including some claimants — with smaller recoveries than a managed restructuring would have produced [S2].

Non-debtor release mechanisms, like the asbestos trusts created under existing bankruptcy law, currently give claimants a structured, guaranteed payout channel in exchange for giving up individual suits; narrowing courts' ability to channel and enjoin claims could leave some claimants with a legal right they can never practically collect [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — stopping companies from using a bankruptcy filing as a shield that freezes injury lawsuits against their parents — is real and long-recognized by courts and Congress alike. The trade-off is genuine: some debtors use corporate restructuring for legitimate reasons, and the bill's four-year lookback and near-irrebuttable presumptions are blunt tools that could deter valid reorganizations. On balance, the bill targets a specific, documented abuse rather than bankruptcy filings generally, and it leaves already-confirmed bankruptcy plans untouched [S2].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on April 20, 2026, and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote since [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) introduced S. 4346 on April 20, 2026, joined by Sens. Josh Hawley (R-MO) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that is the last action on record [S4].
The bill is not yet law and nothing in it takes effect unless it passes both chambers and is signed; previously confirmed bankruptcy plans would remain valid even if it did pass [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the status quo holds: companies that use bankruptcy filings to freeze injury lawsuits against their parent companies keep that tool, at least until Congress acts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies using bankruptcy to stall lawsuits

industries.industry: Mass-tort defendants (large consumer-products and pharmaceutical companies facing talc, asbestos, and similar claims)
industries.note: These companies rely on the bankruptcy stay and non-debtor releases to cap and freeze mass-tort liability. The bill removes that shield for claims involving 100 or more injured people, which is exactly how their interest runs against claimants' ability to sue.

Divisional mergers that move liabilities into a thinly capitalized entity and then file bankruptcy — the so-called Texas Two-Step — would trigger an automatic bad-faith presumption and can no longer be used to cap liability to two or more creditors holding protected claims. Their gain under current law comes at claimants' expense.

Claims against entities whose liability arises from providing insurance to the debtor count as protected claims, so insurers can no longer rely on the bankruptcy stay to keep policyholder lawsuits at bay. Their incentive to avoid payouts conflicts with claimants' ability to recover on legitimate claims.
Lawyers representing injured claimants gain a live path to sue non-debtor parents and insurers, so their financial interest runs alongside their clients' recoveries in this bill.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has only two cosponsors and has sat in the Judiciary Committee without a hearing or markup since its April 2026 referral. Most Senate bills die in committee without floor action, and with roughly eight months left in this Congress, the realistic path is that this bill stalls unless its backers attach it to a larger package or build much broader support.
